items.criterion: ffprobe format duration is within 0.1 s of the 75s the brief committed to.
items.why: brief commits to 75 seconds. A loose tolerance invites padding.
items.check: `ffprobe -show_entries format=duration` → |d − 75.0| ≤ 0.1.

items.criterion: Video stream resolution is exactly 720×1280 (vertical 9:16).
items.why: brief commits to a 720×1280 TikTok deliverable.
items.check: ffprobe width=720, height=1280.

items.criterion: Container is MP4 and the video codec is H.264 (as the brief asks).
items.why: brief commits to an H.264 MP4.
items.check: ffprobe format_name contains "mp4"; stream codec_name == "h264".

items.criterion: Every spoken word in the reel is present in the source broadcast transcript. No newly written narrator script, no TTS voice-over, no rewritten-and-reread commentary. Exception: a reel with no speech at all (crowd + music only) auto-passes.
items.why: the brief says the commentary stays in James and Rune's voice. Rewritten VO defeats the point.
items.check: deterministic — whisper the repurposed cut audio, normalize (lowercase, strip punctuation), chunk into ≥ 4-word phrases; pass iff ≥ 90% of repurpose phrases are substring-findable in `the source transcript` with ≤ 10% character edit-distance tolerance.

items.criterion: No silence-AND-no-crowd stretch runs longer than 1.5s within the content body (first 2s and last 3s excluded).
items.why: dead air breaks the live-session feel. A sports reel needs continuous sonic floor.
items.check: deterministic — librosa RMS on the repurposed cut audio, threshold at −50 dBFS; pass iff no contiguous below-threshold span > 1.5s in [2.0s, runtime − 3.0s].

items.criterion: An audio track is present and non-silent across the full runtime.
items.why: a silent reel fails the genre outright.
items.check: ffprobe shows an audio stream; mean RMS of full track > −55 dBFS.

items.criterion: The first 0.5 seconds don't contain a black-leader / solid-color pad. The reel starts on content.
items.why: brief asks the first five seconds to "earn what comes after". A fade-from-black pad wastes feed attention.
items.check: ffmpeg mean brightness on frame 0.0s, 0.1s, 0.3s; pass iff mean brightness > 15 (on 0-255) at 2 of 3 sampled frames.

items.criterion: The end title card (leaderboard / Simple Session 25 mark) takes up no more than 3.0 seconds of runtime.
items.why: brief asks for "a second or two, not a long pad."
items.check: opus-vision on the last 8 seconds; pass iff the title-card frames (a static graphic with no moving broadcast footage) run ≤ 3.0s continuous.

items.criterion: V-SIGNATURE-PLAY-LANDS  Christopher Kroon's Run 1, specifically the crook-to-bonk 5-0 on the pyramid rail at source ~33:00 (seconds 1975-1982 of the broadcast), is in the reel AND lands. The skater + board + rail are fully within the 9:16 frame at the trick impact, the clip runs ≥ 3.0 continuous seconds so the trick unfolds rather than flashing, AND at least one of (a) Rune's audible call on the trick or the follow-up 85.16 score reveal, (b) the crook-to-5-0 being recognizable as a rail trick not a generic slide, (c) the "85.16" score chyron visible adjacent in time. Not a 0.8-second flash in a montage.
items.why: most-decisive-moment. Kroon's 85.16 is the contest-defining beat. If it's not on screen with weight, the reel has no winner.
items.check: opus-vision on the repurposed cut + source-aligned commentary; pass iff all three conditions (moment present, impact fully framed, ≥ 3s continuous, at least one of the three context proofs).

items.criterion: V-ACTION-CENTERED  The primary action (skater + board + the obstacle being hit) stays within the central 80% of the 9:16 frame across a 1fps sample of action frames. The reframe doesn't park the camera on an empty stripe of arena floor while a trick is happening at the edge.
items.why: vertical reframing is the primary craft risk. A center-crop that loses the skater defeats the reel.
items.check: opus-vision samples repurposed cut at 1 fps; pass iff ≥ 90% of action-present frames (frames where a rider is on course mid-run) have the skater's torso within the central 80% horizontal band of the 9:16 frame.

items.criterion: V-TRACKING-SMOOTH  No visible reframe jitter between cuts and within clips. The reframe center doesn't snap erratically at a play-to-play cut, and the reframe doesn't judder mid-clip as the skater moves.
items.why: a jittery reframe announces the edit and breaks the viewer out of the session.
items.check: opus-vision inspects the six cut-transition frames nearest the content-body midpoint and six mid-clip windows during active tracking; pass iff none of the sampled moments show a jarring reframe snap or mid-clip judder.

items.criterion: V-TRACKING-RESPONSIVE  The reframe follows the skater as they move across the course, not a fixed center. On a traversal clip (skater rolling from rail section to bowl, or from drop-in to box), the reframe tracks with the subject rather than letting them drift to the edge.
items.why: a static center-crop fails Simple Session's course geometry. The course spans a wide 16:9 floor and a good reframe must pan.
items.check: opus-vision on at least one clip ≥ 3s long where the skater traverses laterally; pass iff the skater stays within the central 70% horizontal band across the full traversal.

items.criterion: V-REFRAME-CONSISTENT  The reel uses one reframe strategy throughout (tracking crop OR blur-fill OR center crop OR any single consistent choice). Not a mixed bag that announces the edit.
items.why: mixed strategies make the reel look assembled, not cut.
items.check: opus-vision samples 6 frames evenly across the content body; pass iff all sampled frames show the same reframe strategy.

items.criterion: V-SCOREBOARD-LEGIBLE At least one moment in the reel shows an on-screen score graphic clearly enough that a viewer can read it. This is Kroon's 85.16 reveal, the top-6 standings panel (see `source analysis` `overview/kf_20`), or a rider's post-run score chyron (e.g. the Beaver Fleming 82.50 chyron in `detail/post_040`).
items.why: "what's the score" is a first-order viewer question. Without a legible score, the reel is a stunt compilation, not a contest repurpose.
items.check: opus-vision at 1 fps across the content body; pass iff at least one frame contains a broadcast-native score graphic with numerals clearly readable at 1080×1920 resolution.

items.criterion: V-KEY-RIDER-FRAMED  The skater's face or full-body silhouette is visible and identifiable during the trick impact of each of the reel's top-3 moments. When Kroon's pyramid-rail trick, Fletcher's 84.16 run, or Fleming's backflip-on-the-box hit the key frame, the skater isn't cropped to a disembodied board or a head-only shot.
items.why: a highlight reel that crops riders to anonymous footage loses the "who" that a contest repurpose depends on.
items.check: opus-vision on the peak-impact frame of each of the three signature-run clips in the reel; pass iff the skater's head and torso are visible in at least 2 of 3.

items.criterion: V-OPENS-ON-SUBSTANCE  The first 5 seconds of the reel carry finals content. A visible trick in the broadcast's own call, a rider dropping in, or a commentator call. Not a Red Bull slate, not a Simple Session logo bumper, not a "highlights presented by" sponsor card.
items.why: brief says the first five seconds "have to earn what comes after". A logo intro wastes feed attention on TikTok.
items.check: opus-vision samples frames at 0.0s, 1.5s, 3.0s, 4.5s; pass iff at least 3 of 4 sampled frames show broadcast-source finals content (rider on course, scoreboard, interview, commentator booth), not a full-screen logo / sponsor slate.

items.criterion: V-NO-BAIL-AS-MAKE  A bail or fall isn't cut to imply a landed trick. Specifically: Elias Nilsen's nose-blunt attempt (source ~29:30, transcript 452-459 is a fall, "weight was maybe under it"), and Julian Agliardi's kickflip-backflip-to-backsmith attempt (source ~42:00, transcript 625-626 is a fall, "yeah he's just confused"), if either appears in the reel, must not be cut on the impact frame in a way that suggests the trick was landed.
items.why: moments. Stitching a bail as a make is the most common way a skate reel misrepresents what happened.
items.check: opus-vision on any Nilsen / Agliardi frames in the reel (identify via board-color / jersey / chyron-context); pass iff no falling moment is paired with a title / score chyron / commentary call implying a landed trick.

items.criterion: N-IDENTITY  A cold viewer (scrolling past, knowing nothing about Simple Session) can, from the reel alone, name the winning skater (**Kroon**, with first name either "Kristoffer" per the broadcast chyron or "Christopher" per the commentary rendering, accept either) and the winning score (**85.16**). This is legible from at least two of: audible commentary naming Kroon as the leader, a readable scoreboard / standings frame showing "KROON 85.16" or "KRISTOFFER KROON 85.16," or the end-title card listing the leaderboard with Kroon on top.
items.why: the baseline a contest repurpose owes a viewer. Who won, with what score. Without this, the reel is a skate montage, not a repurposed cut.
items.check: opus-vision + gemini-audio on the repurposed cut; pass iff at least two of (commentary call of "Kroon" / "new leader" / "85.16," readable on-screen Kroon graphic, end-title card with Kroon-1st) are present and legible.

items.criterion: N-ARC  The reel carries the contest's actual arc: Grayson Fletcher posted the first big score of the finals (84.16), Kroon dropped the street-tech run and bumped him out of first with 85.16, and the chase that followed didn't catch him. A viewer should leave able to say in one sentence that "Fletcher led, Kroon took it, the rest couldn't close." The ordering and beat-weighting should reflect this arc, not a flat chronological parade of runs.
items.why: arc. The arc is what makes a repurposed cut more than a scoring compilation. If a viewer can't tell that Kroon came from behind Fletcher, the reel has decayed into clips-next-to-clips.
items.check: opus-vision on repurpose frames at 1 fps + repurpose transcript; pass iff the reel contains both Fletcher's 84.16 beat (run or score chyron) AND Kroon's 85.16 beat (run or score chyron), in that broadcast-true order, with at least one subsequent rider chasing after Kroon.

items.criterion: N-PIVOT-PRESERVED  The "new leader" moment, Kroon's 85.16 score reveal at source 34:58 (seconds 2098-2108) with Rune Glifburg's call "we have a new leader, Christopher Kroon", is in the reel AND given room. The clip around it runs ≥ 3.0 continuous seconds, Rune's call is audible concurrent with either the score chyron or Kroon reacting, and a crowd response is audible. A pivot condensed to a 0.8-second flash isn't preserved.
items.why: most-decisive-moment. The reel's implicit claim that Kroon won is only credible if the moment that made it true is given weight.
items.check: opus-vision + gemini-audio; verify a clip in the reel aligned with source 2098-2108 runs ≥ 3s continuously AND has audible commentary (Rune's call or substring "new leader" or "Kroon" or "85") overlapping.

items.criterion: N-DECISIVE-TRICK  The specific trick Kroon used to seal the run, the **crook-to-bonk 5-0 on the pyramid rail** (source ~33:00, transcript 470), is identifiable in the reel as a rail trick on a specific obstacle. Not a generic slide cut so short it could be any rail from any run.
items.why: moments #1. Rune calls this trick out by name on the broadcast. Preserving it is the difference between a repurposed cut that names the moment and a repurposed cut that just shows a rider winning.
items.check: opus-vision inspects the Kroon clip(s) in the reel; pass iff at least one clip runs ≥ 2.0 continuous seconds on a rail trick where the skater is on the rail in the start-frame and in the land-frame (not just a flying shot or a post-bonk rollaway).

items.criterion: N-NO-FABRICATION  No scoring event or contest-state claim in the reel contradicts the source. Specifically: (a) a score chyron must match the rider shown (Solmunde 71.16, Fleming 82.50, Winberg 83.31, Fletcher 84.16, Kroon 85.16), (b) no end-title card names anyone other than Kroon as the leader / winner after the Kroon beat, (c) no bail is titled as a make (see V-09), (d) Danny Leon doesn't appear next to a "winner" framing (his Run 1 is incomplete in the source file and his score is never announced in the broadcast).
items.why: moments. Stitching skate footage out of order is the most common way a contest repurpose quietly lies about what happened.
items.check: opus-vision cross-references each score chyron / title card / commentary claim in the reel against `source analysis`; pass iff none of (a) — (d) is violated.

items.criterion: N-MULTI-RIDER  At least 3 of the top-6 standings riders (Kroon, Fletcher, Winberg, Fleming, Agliardi, Solmunde) are each shown on at least one distinct trick, run clip, post-run interview, or legible score chyron.
items.why: a one-rider reel reads as a Kroon edit, not a contest repurpose. The brief asks for the chase.
items.check: opus-vision identifies riders via jersey / lower-third / board graphics; pass iff ≥ 3 distinct top-6 riders appear across the reel's content body.

items.criterion: N-SAKURAI-TIMELINE  Issei Sakurai (the #1 qualifier) does NOT appear in the reel framed as a "today's finals" live moment. The broadcast cuts off before Sakurai's finals Run 1. Any Sakurai footage in the reel must either be clearly pre-show / warm-up / qualifier-repurpose context (e.g. the qualifier-repurpose montage at source 1:25-2:30) or a post-run interview he doesn't appear in.
items.why: moments. A reel that presents Sakurai dropping in "today" is a fabrication because the source doesn't contain that footage.
items.check: opus-vision inspects any Sakurai-identified frames in the reel (identified via the chyron in `scoreboard/sb_015` or the qualifier-repurpose context); pass iff none is framed as a live finals trick on run-clock graphic today.

items.criterion: N-NOT-A-BMX-REEL  Footage from the BMX / skate / ice-hockey cross-promo segment (source ~6:00-9:30) and the simple-session-bell best-trick repurpose (source ~4:15-5:30) isn't presented as skate-finals content. If either appears, it is ≤ 2 seconds of repurpose-context / B-roll and isn't mixed into the primary finals sequence without a clear contextual cue.
items.why: moments. Those tangents aren't the skate finals. Pulling from them and presenting them as finals footage is the single largest off-topic risk.
items.check: opus-vision samples all non-skater-on-course footage in the reel; pass iff no BMX shot or the ice-hockey rink is cut into the finals primary sequence (a brief context cue is allowed if titled clearly, not labeled as a finals run).

items.criterion: S-COMMENTARY  The broadcast commentary is audible on Kroon's decisive beat. Specifically Rune Glifburg's "we have a new leader, Christopher Kroon" (source 2098-2108), OR an equivalent commentary call naming Kroon OR naming the 85.16 score is audible on the Kroon footage. A reel that mutes the booth on the moment it is celebrating has thrown away the genre's authority.
items.why: character. Rune's call on Kroon is the single most reel-useful piece of audio in the hour. Muting it turns a contest repurpose into a silent compilation.
items.check: gemini-audio on the repurposed cut audio only; pass iff, over the Kroon-showing window, an audible commentator voice is present AND the transcript of that window contains at least one of {"new leader", "Kroon", "Krune", "Crune", "Kristoffer", "Christopher", "85"}.

items.criterion: S-NO-NARRATOR  No second-narrator voice is laid over the broadcast. The only human voices audible are the broadcast's own: James Threlford / Rune Glifburg in the booth, Tuli F. Stigneov on sideline interviews, the riders themselves in post-run interviews, PA announcer or crowd. No explainer-style VO over the session, no AI-TTS voice reading the leaderboard, no documentary narration.
items.why: character + brief. Collapsing to a narrative-repurpose shape by adding a second narrator voids the reason to watch a sports reel rather than read a results article.
items.check: gemini-audio on the repurposed cut; pass iff the only intelligible human voices are plausibly the broadcast's own (British-English booth, Tuli's sideline-English, riders' interview audio, or crowd), AND there is no studio-acoustic narrator distinct from those.

items.criterion: S-CROWD  Arena crowd ambience is audible across at least one trick-impact beat in the reel. The room reaction on Kroon's crook-to-bonk 5-0, or Fletcher's crowd grab, or Beaver's backflip-on-the-box. The reel doesn't drop the ambient track to run a music-only clip across a signature trick.
items.why: crowd reaction is the sonic anchor that tells a viewer a trick landed. Without it, the reel feels like footage rather than a session.
items.check: gemini-audio on the repurposed cut; pass iff a non-music, non-commentary crowd bed is audible across at least one of the reel's trick-impact windows.

items.criterion: S-SEAM-LEVEL  Cuts don't truncate commentary mid-word, and there's no jarring audio-level drop across a cut. A booth call that starts in one clip should either finish in that clip or cross-fade smoothly.
items.why: a mid-word truncation pulls a viewer out of the session.
items.check: gemini-audio; pass iff no truncation of a commentary word is audible at any cut boundary in the content body.

items.criterion: S-MUSIC-BED-SUBORDINATE  If a music bed is used underneath, it is mixed subordinate to the commentary on key calls. A viewer can clearly hear Rune's "new leader" call over the bed. No music is required. A commentary-plus-crowd reel also passes.
items.why: a music bed that drowns the booth collapses the reel to a silent-edit genre.
items.check: gemini-audio on the Kroon-decisive-beat window; pass iff either (a) no music bed is present on that window, or (b) a music bed is present but the commentary remains intelligible (≥ −6 dB relative to the bed on the call).

items.criterion: S-COMMENTARY-MOOD  Broadcast commentary tone tracks the actual highs of the play. The commentary call rises into the decisive moment and registers the energy of the action; flat reading or wrong-energy commentary (calm voice over the climax, hyped voice over a dead beat) fails this.
items.why: the genre's emotional authority lives in the booth's pacing and intensity. A reel that preserves commentary words but flattens their delivery has thrown away the live-broadcast register the brief asks for.
items.check: gemini-audio on repurpose audio. For each commentary-bearing window, judge whether the commentator's intensity tracks the visual action (rising into the decisive moment, restrained on slower beats). Pass iff no mismatched window (flat reading over a peak, or hyped delivery over a non-event) is observed.

items.criterion: S-VOICE-CONSISTENCY  If the repurposed cut uses broadcast commentary, no audible swap between unrelated commentary teams (no cut from one network's booth to another's). If the repurposed cut adds narration, a single narrator voice is used throughout the content body, with no audible speaker swap.
items.why: commentary identity is part of the broadcast's authority. Stitching two different booths together, or cycling between two narrators, breaks the reel's sonic spine and reads as assembled-from-parts.
items.check: gemini-audio on repurpose audio. Enumerate distinct human voices in the content body. Pass iff (a) all commentary voices match a single broadcast booth (or set of booth voices that always travel together), AND (b) any added narration is delivered by exactly one consistent voice across the reel.

items.criterion: Horizontal black bars (or solid-color bars) occupy more than 30% of frame height for a majority (≥ 50%) of the reel's content body. This is the "lazy reframe" failure. The editor didn't reframe; they letterboxed the 16:9 broadcast into a 9:16 container.
items.why: pillarboxing 16:9 into 9:16 is the single largest reframe failure mode and throws away most of the TikTok deliverable's pixels.
items.check: opus-vision samples repurposed cut frames at 1 fps and measures the vertical extent of contiguous black / near-black / solid-color bars at frame top + frame bottom; fire iff bars > 30% of the 1920-pixel frame height on ≥ 50% of sampled content-body frames.

items.criterion: Horizontal bars occupy 10-30% of frame height on a majority (≥ 50%) of sampled content-body frames. The reel has reframed something but is still wasting visible pixels. Severe and mild are mutually exclusive: a reel that meets the severe threshold does not additionally trigger mild.
items.why: mild pillarboxing still reads as lazy on a vertical feed, even if less egregious than full letterboxing.
items.check: opus-vision on the same sample as P4-PILLARBOX-SEVERE; fire iff 10% ≤ bars ≤ 30% on ≥ 50% of sampled frames AND P4-PILLARBOX-SEVERE didn't fire.

items.criterion: The 16:9 content is visibly squished into 9:16. Aspect-distorted rather than cropped. Skaters look horizontally compressed / vertically stretched. A skateboard deck appears narrower than normal. Heads look elongated. The ratio distortion is readable on ≥ 50% of sampled content-body frames.
items.why: aspect-distorted skaters make the whole reel look amateurishly scaled and are immediately disqualifying on any social platform.
items.check: opus-vision inspects representative rider / board / face shots in the reel (≥ 6 sampled frames across the content body); fire iff proportions are visibly distorted on ≥ 3 of 6 sampled frames.

items.criterion: At ≥ 3 moments in the reel's content body, the action (skater, board, or the obstacle they are hitting) drifts out of or clips at the edge of the 9:16 frame because the reframe didn't follow the play. Different failure mode from pillarbox / squish: the reel has attempted a crop but the crop doesn't track.
items.why: a reframe that loses the action is worse than no reframe at all. The viewer loses the moment the reel is supposed to be delivering.
items.check: opus-vision samples the repurposed cut at 1 fps during action windows (skater-on-course frames); fire iff on ≥ 3 sampled moments the primary subject is at the frame edge (within 10 pixels of the left or right boundary) or completely out of frame while a trick is in progress.
